text: On the 27th of August, 1883, an island in the Sunda Strait began to come apart.
The third blast, at 10:02 that morning, is the loudest sound in recorded history.
Forty miles away, the pressure broke men's eardrums.
A hundred miles off, at Batavia, a gasometer jumped off its trace.
Inside the strait, it did not arrive as sound at all. It arrived as a wall of air.
Then the sea came.
Waves ran a hundred feet high into the towns of the strait.
36,417 people died. Most of them were drowned, not burned.
On Sebesi, eight miles away, three thousand people lived. None survived.
Two thirds of the island fell into the sea, and left a caldera.
A Dutch gunboat, the Berouw, was carried two miles inland.
Nearly three thousand miles away, a harbour master heard what he took for heavy guns.
The air wave kept going. Barographs in London and Washington picked it up.
Stations logged it seven times in five days, as it ran round the planet and came back the other way.
The ash went higher, fifty miles up, and the sunsets went red.
In London, an artist named William Ashcroft sat on the Thames and sketched them, thousands of times.
New York sent fire engines to a fire that was the sky.
The planet cooled by half a degree, and did not warm back for five years.
Krakatoa was the first disaster the telegraph carried round the world in a day.
And in 1927, out of the same water, Anak Krakatau rose.
The loudest thing we have ever heard was an island, dying.
